treatment: Care is led by rheumatology and targets the underlying systemic sclerosis. Painful deposits are sometimes removed surgically.

defects: Image does not support a sufficiently distinct teaching answer: The image shows diffuse periarticular lobulated amorphous calcific deposits at virtually every IP and MCP joint of all five digits, including fingertip tufts. The morphology is fluffy and chalk-like, consistent with calcinosis cutis in systemic sclerosis given the clinical vignette of Raynaud's phenomenon (fingers turning white and numb in the cold), which is a hallmark feature of systemic sclerosis. However, tophaceous gout produces an identical radiographic appearance — multiple periarticular lobulated calcified masses at IP and MCP joints — and cannot be excluded on imaging alone without serum urate levels or synovial fluid analysis. The Raynaud's history increases the prior probability of systemic sclerosis substantially, but the radiographic pattern alone does not discriminate between these two diagnoses. The visible discriminator favouring systemic sclerosis is the clinical context of Raynaud's phenomenon rather than any purely visible radiographic feature, so singleAnswerSupported is false on imaging alone, though the vignette tips the balance toward systemic sclerosis.

findings: Posteroanterior (PA) projection of the right hand, fingers extended and slightly spread

Multiple bilateral periarticular soft-tissue densities with irregular, lobulated, cloud-like calcific deposits clustered around virtually every interphalangeal joint (proximal and distal) of all five digits, as well as the metacarpophalangeal joints; the deposits are most prominent at the fingertip tufts and PIP joints
The calcific deposits have a 'fluffy' or 'chalky' amorphous morphology rather than the smooth, dense appearance of dystrophic or vascular calcification
Underlying cortical bone contours are largely preserved at this level of assessment; no obvious gross destructive lytic or sclerotic osseous lesion is identified beyond periarticular changes
Joint spaces appear relatively maintained in most locations, though several PIP joints show mild narrowing
Thumb interphalangeal joint and MCP joint also show periarticular calcific deposits
Distal phalangeal tufts show some irregular density consistent with soft-tissue calcification at the fingertips
differential: Tophaceous gout: multiple periarticular amorphous/lobulated calcified tophi at virtually every IP and MCP joint is the most characteristic appearance; distribution and morphology are highly consistent

Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) deposition disease: can produce periarticular calcifications, though classically chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage/hyaline cartilage; the lobulated soft-tissue deposits here are less typical but possible

Tumoral calcinosis or hydroxyapatite deposition disease: periarticular cloud-like calcific masses are possible, though the diffuse symmetric multi-joint involvement favors a systemic crystal arthropathy over this diagnosis
anatomyConcerns: A second hand is faintly visible overlapping in the background (lower-left), suggesting superimposition of a second extremity or positioning artifact, which does not affect primary diagnostic assessment
No acquisition or labeling markers visible in the image; laterality assigned based on visual anatomy only
